chapter_theme: Each lover declares what this love is. He makes it a bond of body and life, and she makes it an indwelling so complete that separation is impossible, which leaves the townspeople's talk of an absent, unloving man simply mistaken.
structure_note: Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar divide the chapter by speaker: the man in 1121-1125 and the woman in 1126-1130.

1121.reading: The man says the moisture at the white teeth of this soft-spoken woman is like milk mixed with honey.
1121.nuance: Parimelazhagar notices why the comparison is a mixture and not one sweet thing: milk and honey each have a known taste, while their blend has a sweetness you can't name.

1122.reading: The man says the bond between him and this girl is what the bond between body and life is.
1122.nuance: நட்பு, the word for friendship, is what the verse uses. Parimelazhagar's reading is that these are words for her: she is privately wondering who he is, whether he loves her and whether they will meet again, and he answers what he reads in her face. He files the verse under fear of parting, and Manakkudavar agrees: I can't leave you.

1123.reading: The man tells the image in the pupil of his eye to leave, because there is no room there for the fair-browed woman he loves.
1123.nuance: The conceit depends on the Tamil word for the pupil's reflection, பாவை, a little figure living inside the eye. Parimelazhagar sets this at the moment she is leaving him: since he can't bear not seeing her, she must move in.

1124.reading: The man says the finely jewelled woman is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she goes.
1124.nuance: She isn't compared to life and death as things, but to what happens to a life, its staying in the body and its leaving. Parimelazhagar notes that the ideas of 'for me' and 'in union' have to be supplied, since the verse says only 'when she leaves'.

1125.reading: The man, answering her friend's question whether he remembers them, says he would recall the qualities of the bright-eyed woman if he ever forgot them, but he doesn't know how to forget.
1125.nuance: The answer is a logical joke that turns the friend's question over: remembering presupposes forgetting, so no, he never thinks of her. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both mark this as the end of the man's speech.

1126.reading: The woman says her lover won't leave her eyes and isn't hurt even if she blinks, so subtle is he.
1126.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives this a strategic setting: she fears her friend will blame the absent man, and speaks to herself so that the friend will overhear. Her defence of him is that he hasn't gone anywhere. The invisible subtle body sounds like metaphysics, but he explains it as ceaseless thinking grown so ripe that the man is always before her.

1127.reading: The woman says that since her lover lives in her eyes, she doesn't even line them with kohl, knowing he would be hidden.
1127.nuance: A real sign of separation, an unadorned face, is given a loving explanation. Manakkudavar adds a second one: she is so busy watching him within that she has no time to dress.

1128.reading: The woman says that since her lover lives in her heart, she is afraid to eat hot food, knowing he would be burned.
1128.nuance: Manakkudavar supplies the occasion: her friend has asked why she isn't eating. Loss of appetite is one of the visible symptoms, and this is a graceful evasion of the question.

1129.reading: The woman says she won't blink, knowing he would be hidden, and for this much the town calls him loveless.
1129.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a quarrel behind 'this town': the friend has criticised the man to help her endure, and she, hurt, refuses to name the friend, calling her the town. Sleeplessness, the very evidence against him, she presents as her own act of care.

1130.reading: The woman says he lives joyfully in her heart always, while this town says he is loveless and lives apart.
1130.nuance: The last words are identical to 1129's, and the refrain suggests how worn out she is by this argument. Whether her certainty is comfort or denial, the verse doesn't say.

links.note: Both use the same phrase for the friendship of body and life. In 338 it is like a bird flying from an abandoned shell, an image of how easily it ends. In 1122 it is the lover's image for an unbreakable bond. The thing he swears by is what the book on renunciation calls fragile, and in 1124 he seems to know it.

He says 'I don't know forgetting' with a clever smile. In 1207 the woman uses the same words, மறப்பறியேன், and adds that even remembering burns her. The same claim of constant memory is banter for one and torment for the other.
Here the town's talk is a misunderstanding she can rebut. In 1147, the talk has become manure for the love itself. Her stance towards gossip shifts from defence to using it.

source_issues: 1126: The verse text has பருகுவரா, while Parimelazhagar and Pope read it as பருவரார், 'won't suffer'. பருகுவரா looks like a corruption of the source text.
1130: The verse text has இகந்து, while Parimelazhagar glosses இகழ்ந்து.
